newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan forex reform may not cause outflow--Dai-ichi.
newsitem.headline: Japan forex reform may not cause outflow--Dai-ichi.

text.p: Revisions in Japan's foreign exchange law may not necessarily result in an exodus of Japanese capital to overseas markets, Dai-ichi Life Research Institute Inc said in a report on Tuesday.
Capital flows into and out of Japan after the implementation of forex deregulation is more likely to depend on foreign exchange rates and interest rates at that time, it said.
Dai-ichi Life Research is a unit of Japan's second-largest life insurer, Dai-ichi Mutual Life Insurance Co.
Drastic reforms of the Foreign Exchange and Foreign Trade Control Law, passed by parliament in May, will come into effect in April 1998.

The lifting of controls on foreign exchange transactions in Britain in October 1979 resulted in rapid net capital outflows, but the British experience may not necessarily apply to Japan, Dai-ichi said.

This is partly because forex controls were virtually scrapped overnight in Britain, while the bulk of regulations concerning institutional investors have already been eliminated in Japan, Dai-ichi said.
Dai-ichi said its studies show that forex deregulation does not just result in a larger capital outflow but also more capital inflow.
It said France experienced an increase in net capital inflows after forex deregulation was implemented between 1985 and 1990.
Whether or not capital outflows would be greater than capital inflows would largely depend on interest rates and forex rates, Dai-ichi said.

France at the time of forex deregulation was facing rising interest rates and a strong franc. By contrast, Britain had negative real interest rates and sterling was weaker in the period after its scrapping of forex controls, Dai-ichi said.
Japan's forex law revisions will eliminate numerous regulations concerning cross-border transactions and allow corporations and individuals to deal directly with overseas banks and brokers.
Some experts say that the revisions could trigger a rapid outflow of Japanese capital without more deregulation in Japanese financial markets.
